extracted.intended_audience: advertisers, advertising historians, students and practitioners of media buying
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative principles for choosing, placing, and pricing newspaper advertisements (historical perspective). Focuses on matching ads to readership, cost considerations, media reputation, and tactical choices like position and repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place advertisement where target readers will see it
rubrics_metrics.description: "the essence of advertising is to place your statement where it is most likely to be seen by those most interested in it","no matter how extensive a circulation may be, it is intrinsically useless unless flowing through the channel which is fairly likely to effect the purpose for which the advertisement is inserted.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose newspapers or sections whose readership matches the intended customer class; a small-circulation paper that reaches the right audience can be more valuable than a large, irrelevant circulation. Consider read patterns (who actually reads a detached sheet of ads) when deciding placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat circulation as only partial evidence of value
rubrics_metrics.description: "actual circulation but not as a whole, sole, and complete qualification.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not select media solely by raw circulation numbers. Use circulation as one indicator among others (demographic fit, reader interests, position, editorial alignment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pay for position or special insertion when justified
rubrics_metrics.description: "they pay extra for position or insertion, they know that their outlay is remunerative.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professional advertisers and experienced buyers often pay premiums for advantageous positions (e.g., above-the-fold, front columns, special sections) because these placements increase ad effectiveness and return on investment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan and regulate advertising expenditure strategically
rubrics_metrics.description: "advertising is a most expensive luxury if not properly regulated, and a most valuable adjunct when coolness and calculation are brought to bear upon it as accessories.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt budgeting, testing, and systematic media-planning practices; avoid ad hoc or emotionally driven buys. Consider cost-per-response and monitor outcomes to avoid waste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid placing ads in sections unlikely to be read by desired customers
rubrics_metrics.description: example: "a sheet, detached from the paper with which it is issued, full of advertisements, which are, of course, unread by all but those who are professedly readers of public announcements",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid dumping ads into peripheral or specialized advertising sheets that most of the paper's audience ignores. Match ad location to reader behavior to ensure visibility and readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use trade-specific or specialist publications for niche markets
rubrics_metrics.description: example: the Morning Advertiser "as the organ of the licensed victuallers... in it are to be found advertisements of everything to be obtained in connection with the distillery, the brewery, and the tavern.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When targeting industry-specific customers (e.g., trades, professions), select specialist journals or trade papers where the audience concentration increases response and relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for pricing structure, taxes, and their effect on ad format
rubrics_metrics.description: historical observation: high stamp duties and advertisement taxes "narrowed the limits of their application" and charged per advertisement causing different formatting decisions (e.g., not cutting long ads into separate pieces because of per-ad charges).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand how publishers charge (per line, per column, per insertion, supplements) and how taxes/fees affect the cost of length and frequency. Structure ads to minimize avoidable charges and exploit favorable rate schedules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider supplementary charges and their impact
rubrics_metrics.description: "An additional halfpenny was also charged on a supplement... as an indirect tax on advertisements.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of extra fees for supplements, special editions, or postal wrappers; such surcharges can materially change the economics of a campaign and the desirable format (main paper vs supplement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate media reputation, editorial ethics, and reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: critique of some U.S. papers: editorial columns "are to be bought for any purpose..." and references to deliberate blackmailing practices in provincial papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a newspaper's editorial practices or reputation could harm the advertiser's brand or undermine message credibility. Avoid media known for unethical practices or pay-for-editorial arrangements unless brand alignment is intentionally commercial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use repetition and cross-publication to increase reach
rubrics_metrics.description: example: the Standard "offers to advertisers a repetition of their notices in the Evening Standard.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where available, plan repeat insertions or cross-publication (morning + evening editions, syndicated runs) to increase exposure and reinforce the message across different reading occasions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negotiate rates or use advertisement agents for bulk/agency deals
rubrics_metrics.description: historical note: early Telegraph proprietors closed with advertisement agents who "agreed to take so many columns a day at the then trade price", producing long-term bargains for agents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage volume buying, agency relationships, or negotiated deals to secure lower effective CPM/CPR. Investigate agency packages and historical rate structures to identify advantageous purchasing strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match media geography and market to the advertiser's needs
rubrics_metrics.description: observations: provincial, colonial, and American newspapers each have different strengths—provincials may be more remunerative for certain purposes; colonial papers can be valuable for local colonial audiences; American papers rely heavily on ads and telegraph-fed news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose between national, provincial, colonial/foreign, and local papers based on where the product's customers are located and how they consume news. Localized or colonial outlets may outperform national titles for region-specific products or services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider content mix and editorial focus (news-heavy vs ad-heavy)
rubrics_metrics.description: commentary: some American journals "sacrifice... everything to news" while others have pages "full of advertisements"; this affects the tone and the kinds of ads accepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how the balance of news vs advertising, and the paper's editorial focus, influence reader attention and ad effectiveness. News-heavy papers may attract different reader intents than ad-heavy or classified-driven titles.
